Economy: Japan Q3 GDP -0.1%; BoE's Pill signals more hikes; Bangladesh garment strike; EV makers after midterms. stories.headline: Japan's economy unexpectedly shrinks for the first time in a year
stories.dek: Third-quarter GDP fell 0.1% (annualized) after energy subsidies ended and squeezed shoppers.
stories.caveman: GDP is the total value of everything a country makes and sells. Japan, the world's fourth-biggest economy, reported on Monday that its GDP shrank at an annualized pace of 0.1% in July to September, compared with the quarter before. Experts in a Reuters poll had expected growth of 0.3%. The previous quarter had grown 1.4%. The main reason given: government help with energy bills ran out, so families had less money left for shopping, and spending slowed. Oil and gas prices are high because of the war involving Iran.
stories.why_it_matters: Japan is a giant buyer of chips and parts from Taiwan and the region. When its shoppers pull back, factories across Asia feel it.
stories.camps: Some economists say one weak quarter is a blip and Japan's wages are rising. Others say high energy costs and an aging population keep Japan's growth fragile, and that ending subsidies too early hurt ordinary households.
stories.image_alt: Shipping containers stacked at a port (Getty photo used by CNBC)
stories.image_credit: Photo: Stanislav Kogiku/Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services a country produces.
A quarter-long change stretched out to show what it would be over a full year.
Money the government pays to lower a price for people or companies.

stories.headline: Bank of England's chief economist says more rate rises are likely, starting next month
stories.dek: Huw Pill says 'we have further to go' as UK inflation could hit 5% next spring. About 2.3 million homeowners face pricier mortgages.
stories.caveman: A central bank sets the basic interest rate for a country. Higher rates make borrowing cost more, which slows spending and helps bring prices down. Earlier this month the Bank of England raised its rate from 3.75% to 4%. Now its chief economist, Huw Pill, says it will probably need to raise again in December and in early 2027. He worries inflation could reach 5% next spring because oil and gas are expensive due to the Iran war, and workers may ask for big raises to keep up. He thinks peace and cheaper energy soon are 'very low probability.' He even said, 'we waited too long.' About 2.3 million UK homeowners must renew their mortgages next year and will likely pay more.
stories.why_it_matters: Rate hikes in big economies push up borrowing costs worldwide and can pull money away from stocks, including in Asia.
stories.camps: Pill and other 'hawks' say acting now stops inflation from getting stuck. Critics say higher rates hurt homeowners and renters who did nothing to cause an energy shock, and could tip the economy into a slowdown.
stories.image_alt: The Bank of England building in London

terms.explain: The public bank that sets a country's main interest rate and manages its money.
When prices across the economy keep rising.
A loan used to buy a home.
A policymaker who favors higher rates to fight inflation.

stories.headline: Nearly 150 garment factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike for a higher minimum wage
stories.dek: Workers want 30,000 taka (about £182) a month, up from 12,500. They make clothes for H&M, Primark and Zara.
stories.caveman: Bangladesh is the world's second-biggest exporter of ready-made clothes after China. About four million people work in its garment factories, and clothing brings in nearly $40 billion a year. Workers say the minimum wage of 12,500 taka a month is not enough as prices rise, and they want 30,000 taka. This weekend almost 150 factories closed in the hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur. On Sunday, workers blocked a highway for about an hour until police stepped in. Factory owners' groups say they will keep closed factories shut indefinitely under a 'No Work No Pay' rule. A government wage board set up on 1 November says it will finish its recommendation by the end of November, with new pay expected from 1 December.
stories.why_it_matters: Many clothes in your closet may be made in Bangladesh. How much the workers earn is a question of fairness that reaches all the way to store prices.
stories.camps: Workers and labor groups say big brands make huge profits while the people sewing clothes can't afford food. Factory owners say higher wages could make them lose orders to cheaper countries and want protection from unrest.
stories.image_alt: Garment workers protest in Dhaka demanding a new minimum wage

terms.explain: The lowest pay employers are legally allowed to give workers.
Bangladesh's currency.
A government panel that recommends pay levels for an industry.
When workers stop working together to push for better pay or conditions.

stories.headline: US electric-car bosses say they aren't counting on Democrats to bring back EV help
stories.dek: Democrats won Congress, but Rivian, Lucid and Scout CEOs plan as if no new federal support is coming.
stories.caveman: Under President Biden, buyers got up to $7,500 in tax credit for an electric vehicle (EV). The Trump administration ended or rolled back that help. Now Democrats have won control of Congress, which starts in January. But the bosses of EV makers Rivian, Lucid and Scout Motors told CNBC they are not planning on new support. Rivian's RJ Scaringe said it will probably have 'less of an impact than we think.' Lucid's CEO said, 'Plan for the worst and hope for the best.' One reason: Democrats seem focused first on healthcare subsidies, Medicaid cuts, data centers and the cost of living, and Republican President Trump can still veto bills.
stories.why_it_matters: Electric cars matter for climate change and for battery and chip suppliers, including in Taiwan. Policy flip-flops make companies cautious about investing.
stories.camps: Climate advocates want Democrats to restore EV incentives quickly. Others, including some Democrats, say voters care more about health costs and prices right now, and that EV makers should stand on their own without subsidies.
stories.image_alt: A person charging an electric car at a charging station at night (AFP/Getty photo used by CNBC)

terms.explain: Electric vehicle: a car that runs on a battery instead of gasoline.
Money taken off the tax you owe, used to encourage certain purchases.
When the president refuses to sign a bill passed by Congress.
US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term.

stories.headline: Treasury Secretary Bessent calls for a 'dramatic shakeup' at Nvidia and an outside CEO
stories.dek: He asked whether Nvidia pushed 'seemingly illicit' chip sales to boost earnings, and questioned its Singapore revenue reporting.
stories.caveman: Nvidia makes the chips that power most AI. Its CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore firm Megaspeed whom US intelligence suspects of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of sending Nvidia chips to China against US export rules. Finance chief Colette Kress is interim CEO. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News Nvidia's board should pick a new boss from outside the company, and that other executives should be examined too. 'If this were a bank... a lot of the executives would be removed,' he said. He also pointed to a jump in Nvidia's reported Singapore sales while China sales fell. Bessent is also feuding with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department controls the export blacklist.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia's troubles shake the whole AI industry and Taiwan's chip suppliers. A US government push into who runs a private company is also unusual.
stories.camps: Supporters of Bessent say national security comes first and Nvidia must prove it followed the rules. Critics note the administration's own Commerce Department is under fire, and say officials shouldn't dictate a private company's hiring. Nvidia has not been charged with wrongdoing.
stories.image_alt: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaking at a podium (Getty photo used by CNBC)

terms.explain: Government rules that stop certain products, like advanced chips, from being sold to some countries.
A temporary company boss until a permanent one is chosen.
The group of directors that oversees a company and picks its CEO.

stories.headline: Megaspeed says suspected spy Alice Huang left in 2025; Jensen Huang agrees to testify to Congress
stories.dek: The Singapore chip buyer opened an internal probe. Some tech leaders, including Elon Musk, are lobbying for Huang's return.
stories.caveman: Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia. On Sunday it said Alice Huang left her executive job there in August last year. It called media claims about its business 'not supported by verifiable evidence' and hired outside lawyers to investigate itself. Also on Sunday, Congressman John Moolenaar, who leads the House committee on China, said Jensen Huang agreed to testify before three House committees, behind closed doors. Moolenaar wants to know whether a suspected Chinese spy got secret information or influenced Nvidia's thinking on AI and export rules. Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported Huang was discussing a comeback, and a group of tech leaders including Elon Musk has been rallying support for him.
stories.why_it_matters: The case tests how well the US can keep its most advanced AI chips from China, a fight where Taiwan's factories sit in the middle.
stories.camps: Huang's backers say Nvidia needs its founder and the private scandal shouldn't end his career. Lawmakers from both parties say security questions must be answered first. Many claims remain unproven and are still under investigation.
stories.image_alt: Jensen Huang and Alice Huang at an event (Reuters photo used by BBC)

terms.explain: To answer questions officially, often under oath, before a court or lawmakers.
When a company looks into its own possible problems, often with outside lawyers.
A special group of lawmakers set up to study one topic.

stories.headline: A router installed during a copper-to-fiber upgrade caused the biggest US flight grounding since 9/11
stories.dek: It flooded air traffic control with 1,000 connection attempts every few seconds. Finding it took 45 minutes because maintenance logs are on paper.
stories.caveman: On Friday, all US flights were grounded for more than four hours. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a contractor, L3Harris, was replacing very old copper phone lines with fiber at a remote site and installed a router, a box that directs internet traffic. That router began flooding the air traffic control network with about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. Voice and ground communications became unstable at 17 of 22 regional control centers. It took the FAA 45 minutes to find the source, partly because maintenance work is still logged by hand on paper. Officials said there was no sign of a cyber-attack. Duffy said the system needs a full overhaul costing about $50 billion. Thousands of flights were still cancelled or delayed days later.
stories.why_it_matters: Old public tech can break in big ways. Air travel, banks and power grids all depend on systems that are often decades old.
stories.camps: The Trump administration blames past presidents and Congress for underfunding the system. Critics point to the current administration's own oversight and contractor management. Many agree the network badly needs money, but disagree on who should be held responsible.
stories.image_alt: Stranded passengers waiting with luggage in an airport terminal

terms.explain: An order that keeps all planes on the ground until it is lifted.
A device that directs data traffic between computers on a network.
Federal Aviation Administration, the US agency that runs air traffic control.
Fiber-optic cable that carries data as light; faster than old copper wire.

stories.headline: Anthropic's giant IPO, expected Thursday, is a big test for a shaky AI market
stories.dek: Shares are priced at $70–78. The Claude maker has over $900 billion in spending promises and lost $104 billion in nine months.
stories.caveman: An IPO is when a private company first sells shares to the public. Anthropic, the company behind the AI assistant Claude, is expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday at about $70 to $78 a share. It could raise more than $90 billion. Big tech firms, including Nvidia, Google, Microsoft, Broadcom, AMD, Micron and Taiwan's TSMC, are investing a combined $26 billion at the IPO price. Anthropic has promised to spend over $900 billion on computing, including at least $110 billion with Amazon over ten years. It lost $104 billion in the first nine months of 2026. The IPO arrives as rising interest rates, an AI backlash and Nvidia's leadership crisis weigh on tech stocks.
stories.why_it_matters: If the IPO goes well, it could calm nerves about AI. If it flops, chipmakers and their suppliers, including in Taiwan, could take a hit.
stories.camps: Bulls say Anthropic's fast-growing business proves AI demand is real. Skeptics say spending far outruns income, and that so many companies depending on a few AI labs is risky for the whole market.
stories.image_alt: A business executive walking with security staff (AFP/Getty photo used by CNBC for the Anthropic story)

terms.explain: Initial public offering: the first time a company sells shares to the public.
A big US stock exchange known for tech companies.
When a company spends more than it earns over a period.
The official document a company publishes before an IPO describing its business and risks.

stories.headline: Iran launches drones at a US base in Bahrain for the second time in three days
stories.dek: Bahrain says it shot them down. Iran also claims a mine sank an oil supertanker in the Strait of Hormuz — not independently confirmed.
stories.caveman: The US and Israel started attacking Iran in February, and the conflict is stuck. The US is blockading Iran's sea trade, and Iran is choking ship traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea lane that carries much of the world's oil. On Sunday Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they fired six drones at a US radar at a helicopter base in Bahrain, in revenge for recent US strikes. Bahrain said its air defenses stopped them. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi fighters advanced in the south. Iran also claimed two ships hit mines and one supertanker carrying 2 million barrels sank; there was no independent confirmation. Trump has said the US no longer seeks a deal with Iran.
stories.why_it_matters: This war is a big reason oil, gas and prices are high around the world, including in Taiwan.
stories.camps: Hawks in the US say pressure on Iran must continue. Gulf states have urged Trump to avoid a large war, and critics, including Vice-President Vance after the midterms, have blamed the war for hurting Americans. Iran says it is only responding to US attacks.
stories.image_alt: Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei at a press conference

terms.explain: A narrow sea passage near Iran that much of the world's oil passes through.
Iran's powerful military force that answers to its supreme leader.
An armed group in Yemen backed by Iran.
Using ships or forces to stop goods from going in or out.

stories.headline: Estonia will close all border crossings with Russia after a foiled attack on a drone maker
stories.dek: Eight people were detained trying to bomb and burn Threod Systems. Estonia blames Russia's GRU spy agency.
stories.caveman: Estonia is a small country next to Russia and a member of NATO and the EU. On Saturday, security guards stopped an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a company that makes long-range drones. Eight people were detained, and no one was hurt. Estonia's security service says the aim was to cause an explosion and set the building on fire, and that it was ordered by the GRU, Russia's military intelligence. It is the second attack on an Estonian defense firm blamed on Russia this year. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said all three crossings with Russia will close from 1 December. He said Russia wants to scare Estonia into giving Ukraine less help, but 'Estonia's response is the opposite.'
stories.why_it_matters: Europe is seeing more sabotage blamed on Russia. Closing a border is a big step that also hurts families and trade across it.
stories.camps: Estonia's government says closing the border is needed for security. Some residents of border towns like Narva, many of them Russian speakers, may lose easy contact with relatives. Russia usually denies such accusations.
stories.image_alt: A border checkpoint at Narva on the Estonia–Russia border

terms.explain: Russia's military intelligence agency.
Secretly damaging or destroying something to weaken an enemy.
A military alliance of Europe and North America that promises to defend each other.

stories.headline: Over 350,000 Czechs rally in Prague to defend independent public TV and radio
stories.dek: The government wants to scrap licence fees and pay broadcasters from the state budget. Protesters fear ministers will gain control over news.
stories.caveman: Public broadcasters are TV and radio stations owned by the public, meant to be independent from politicians. In Czechia, they are funded by a fee that households pay. Prime Minister Andrej Babiš's government — a coalition of populist, hard-right and Eurosceptic parties — wants to end the fee and fund them from the state budget instead. On Sunday, organisers said more than 350,000 people rallied at Letná Plain in Prague, where the 1989 Velvet Revolution against communism began. Many wore paper hats like Večerníček, a children's TV bedtime mascot. Protesters say budget funding would let ministers pressure newsrooms, like what happened in Hungary and Slovakia. Staff at Czech TV and Radio have already gone on strike.
stories.why_it_matters: A free press lets people check on those in power. Taiwan also debates how to fund public media without political strings.
stories.camps: The government says ending the fee saves households money. Critics say the real effect is more political control over journalism. Media-freedom groups across Europe are watching closely.
stories.image_alt: Crowds with Czech flags and banners at Letná Plain in Prague

terms.explain: A TV or radio service paid for by the public and meant to be independent.
A charge households pay to fund public broadcasting.
A politician or party that says it speaks for ordinary people against elites.
The peaceful 1989 protests that ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin to meet at APEC in Shenzhen this week, part of a run of Asian summits
stories.dek: Some compare it to 1945's Yalta conference. Analysts say a deal over Ukraine and Taiwan without them is unlikely.
stories.caveman: APEC is a club of Pacific Rim economies that together make up more than 60% of world GDP. This week its leaders meet in Shenzhen, China's tech hub, and Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin have confirmed a three-way meeting. Some people compare it to Yalta in 1945, when US, British and Soviet leaders divided up postwar Europe. One analyst said the meeting may be 'more symbolic than substantive': Trump seems interested in nuclear arms control, Xi wants steady ties with the US, and Putin wants leverage over Ukraine. Before APEC, Trump attends the ASEAN summit in the Philippines, where protesters objected to his visit. The trip comes two weeks after Trump's party lost the midterms.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan is not at the table. Any big-power talk that touches Taiwan matters directly for its future and safety.
stories.camps: Supporters of talks say leaders meeting face to face can lower the risk of war. Critics in Europe and Ukraine worry about deals made over smaller countries' heads, while Australia's leader welcomed the meeting.
stories.image_alt: APEC China 2026 signs and flower beds along a street in Shenzhen

terms.explain: Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a forum of 21 Pacific Rim economies.
Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a group of 10-plus Southeast Asian countries.
The 1945 meeting where Allied leaders shaped postwar Europe.
Deals between countries to limit weapons, especially nuclear ones.

stories.headline: Hot: literary agents turn into influencers, selling advice on Substack, TikTok and in books
stories.dek: Agents like Kate McKean are demystifying publishing for frustrated writers — and building personal brands.
stories.caveman: A literary agent is the person who helps a writer get a book deal with a publisher and takes a cut. The New York Times reports that more agents now share insider advice publicly: newsletters on Substack, TikTok videos, podcasts and how-to books. Agent Kate McKean, author of the guidebook 'Write Through It,' hosts Q&A nights at Liz's Book Bar in Brooklyn. Aspiring authors ask how to stand out, whether social media matters and when to send a manuscript. One writer told her about nearly 800 rejections. McKean's blunt answer: publishing is a business. 'You don't get a book deal because you deserve it.'
stories.why_it_matters: Who's hot right now isn't only authors. The gatekeepers are becoming public figures too, which changes who gets heard.
stories.camps: Fans say this openness helps outsiders who don't have industry connections. Skeptics worry agents spend time building their own brands and that it can turn writing dreams into another paid product.
stories.image_alt: Literary agent Kate McKean
stories.image_credit: Photo: Lila Barth for The New York Times

terms.explain: A professional who sells a writer's book to publishers and negotiates the deal.
A platform where writers publish paid or free email newsletters.
The full draft of a book before it is published.
A short letter a writer sends to agents to pitch a book.

stories.headline: Hot again: fan fiction giant AO3 comes back online, and readers rush back
stories.dek: The volunteer-run archive of nearly 19 million stories was down for more than two weeks after a 'security incident.'
stories.caveman: Fan fiction is stories fans write using characters from books, films or shows they love, like 'Harry Potter' or 'Heated Rivalry.' AO3, short for Archive of Our Own, is the biggest home for it: nearly 19 million works and 12 million users. It is non-profit and run entirely by volunteers. More than two weeks ago a 'security incident' knocked it offline. Volunteers promised no work was lost and said it would return in four weeks. On Sunday it was mostly back, earlier than expected, with some features switched off. AO3 has not said exactly what happened. A Toronto culture writer said the outage showed how deeply shared, fan-made storytelling is now part of everyday life.
stories.why_it_matters: Many young readers and writers learn to write on AO3. Its return shows how much community-run spaces matter next to big companies.
stories.camps: Fans call AO3 a free library made by the people. Some authors and publishers have long debated how fan works relate to copyright, though AO3 operates as non-commercial transformative work.
stories.image_alt: The AO3 website on a screen, showing a notice about restored features

terms.explain: Stories written by fans using characters or worlds from existing works.
Archive of Our Own, a non-profit fan fiction website.
An organization that does not aim to make money for owners.

stories.headline: Hot: a 'Moby-Dick' bar in Manhattan with its own book club, as Melville's novel turns 175
stories.dek: Quick Eternity, near South Street Seaport, takes its décor, drinks and conversation from the great American whale tale.
stories.caveman: 'Moby-Dick' is Herman Melville's huge 1851 novel about Captain Ahab hunting a white whale. It turns 175 this year. Bartender Bryan Schneider was obsessed for ten years with the book's description of a dark, ship-like inn called the Spouter-Inn. In 2025 he opened a cocktail bar called Quick Eternity on Peck Slip, a cobblestone street near New York's old docks. The name comes from a Melville line about death in whaling. Everything is inspired by the book, and his wife, Rachel Leal, runs a book club and other reading events there. Schneider jokes that the bar is his own 'white whale.'
stories.why_it_matters: Classic books are finding new life in social places like bars and clubs, which helps people read hard books together.
stories.camps: Book lovers enjoy the playful mix of literature and nightlife. Some critics say themed venues can turn serious books into décor, but organisers say the club gets people to actually read them.
stories.image_alt: Cocktails and an open book on a table at Quick Eternity
stories.image_credit: Photo: Amir Hamja for The New York Times

terms.explain: Herman Melville's 1851 novel about a sea captain chasing a white whale.
An obsession or goal someone chases for a long time.
A group that reads the same book and meets to talk about it.

stories.headline: Not so hot: used-book seller Alibris strikes a deal to list over a million books on Temu
stories.dek: Books will be stored and shipped in the US. Lit Hub calls it dispiriting to see everything funneled into the same few giant stores.
stories.caveman: Alibris is a US website that sells used and rare books from many small sellers. Publishers Weekly reported it signed a deal to put more than a million books on Temu, the giant discount shopping app. The books will be sourced, stored and shipped locally in the US through Temu's Local Seller program. Alibris also partnered with fast-fashion brand Shein last year. Lit Hub's James Folta notes Temu is known for cheap quality and knock-offs, and has faced accusations about data privacy, intellectual property and a high risk of forced labor in its supply chain, according to a congressional study. He understands the business logic against Amazon, but finds it sad to see even used books squeezed into the same few platforms.
stories.why_it_matters: Where we buy books shapes which booksellers survive. Small sellers may gain buyers, but readers may lose diversity.
stories.camps: Supporters say more places to buy cheap used books is good for readers and small sellers. Critics worry about Temu's record and that independent bookshops lose out as everything moves to mega-platforms.
stories.image_alt: Alibris and Temu logos in a repeating pattern

terms.explain: A Chinese-owned online discount marketplace.
Cheap clothing made quickly in huge amounts to follow trends.
Work people are made to do against their will.
Second-hand books sold again after someone owned them.

stories.headline: England and Wales pardon about 150 women ever investigated for ending their own pregnancies
stories.dek: A new law took effect Monday, wiping records going back 150 years. Some women also want an official apology.
stories.caveman: In England and Wales, abortion is legal within rules, but for a very long time a woman who ended her own pregnancy outside those rules could be prosecuted. Parliament earlier voted to stop treating women this way in the future. Now a law, section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, pardons every woman who faced a criminal investigation for this in the last 150 years. Police records of arrests, cautions and convictions will be deleted, so about 150 women can work and travel freely. Several were prosecuted after getting pills online during Covid. Some were victims of domestic abuse, pushed by partners. Nicola Packer, cleared by a jury last year, said, 'none of us should have been on trial.'
stories.why_it_matters: Women's health and rights are a big part of social justice. Taiwan also debates how law treats pregnancy and reproductive choice.
stories.camps: Campaigners call it historic and want a government apology too. Some anti-abortion groups oppose removing criminal penalties, saying it weakens protection for late pregnancies. The legal time limits for abortion remain in place.
stories.image_alt: Campaigners outside the Royal Courts of Justice in London in 2023

terms.explain: An official decision that forgives a crime and removes its punishment.
To delete a criminal record completely.
A pattern of abuse where a partner controls someone's life through threats and pressure.

stories.headline: World's top court rules Thursday on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
stories.dek: The ICJ has never found a country responsible for genocide. The ruling could shape the separate case against Israel.
stories.caveman: The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority in Myanmar. Nearly ten years ago, Myanmar's military attacked their villages and hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh, where many still live in huge camps in Cox's Bazar. The Gambia, a Muslim-majority African country, took Myanmar to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, saying it broke the 1948 Genocide Convention. Judges have spent seven years on the case and will rule on Thursday. Genocide means acts meant to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, and proving that 'intent' is hard. Lawyers for survivors say villages were attacked the same way again and again: killings, burning homes, separating men and women, and sexual violence.
stories.why_it_matters: It could set the modern standard for the worst crime in international law, and decide whether survivors get justice.
stories.camps: Survivors and rights groups hope the court holds Myanmar fully accountable. Myanmar's military has denied genocide, saying it was fighting armed groups. Legal experts say the bar for proving intent is very high.
stories.image_alt: Rohingya refugees in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, at a genocide remembrance day

terms.explain: Acts meant to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
International Court of Justice, the UN's top court for disputes between countries.
A mostly Muslim minority group from Myanmar.
A person forced to flee their country because of war or persecution.

stories.headline: One year in, New Mexico's free childcare for all is life-changing — if you can get a spot
stories.dek: It's the first US state to offer free childcare regardless of income. One Santa Fe center has nearly 700 kids on its waitlist.
stories.caveman: A year ago, New Mexico became the first US state to make childcare free for every family, no matter how much they earn. Families just need to live there, and adults must be working, looking for work, studying or unable to work. Parents like Judyn Martinez told NPR it changed their lives. But there aren't enough places or workers. Martinez waited about a year and a half for a spot; the center's list now has almost 700 children. Another mom, a children's librarian, was on six waitlists at once. About half of the state's 67,000 kids aged five and under are in the program. Officials admit it needs to grow, and the same shortage of childcare workers exists across the country.
stories.why_it_matters: Childcare cost is a big reason people delay having kids. Taiwan, with very low birth rates, faces the same question.
stories.camps: Supporters say universal childcare helps parents work and children learn. Critics say the state promised more than it could deliver and that free care without enough staff creates long waits.
stories.image_alt: Children in Halloween costumes play at Kids Campus in Santa Fe, New Mexico

terms.explain: Childcare available to all families, not just low-income ones.
A list of people waiting for a spot to open.
A long-running US federal program offering free early education for low-income kids.

stories.headline: Australia, UK, Canada and Italy urge Israel to let 150,000 tents into Gaza before winter
stories.dek: Storms have flooded tents and killed at least four children and a woman. The ministers say the crisis is 'entirely reversible.'
stories.caveman: Gaza has been devastated by war, and most people there live in tents. In the past week, storms soaked and broke thousands of them, and at least four Palestinian children and a woman were killed by heavy rain and wind. On Monday, the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the UK called the situation 'dire' and asked Israel to stop delays and let 150,000 tents and other supplies waiting at the border into Gaza. They also asked for 'dual-use' items needed for aid work. In Australia, Greens leader David Shoebridge said strong words aren't enough and called for sanctions and an end to arms trade with Israel.
stories.why_it_matters: Winter makes a humanitarian disaster deadlier. How allies pressure Israel is one of the biggest moral debates in world politics.
stories.camps: Aid groups and many governments say Israel must open crossings now. Israel has said it restricts some 'dual-use' goods because they could be used by Hamas. Activists say joint statements without sanctions change little.
stories.image_alt: Palestinian children carrying pots in Gaza

terms.explain: Help like food, water, shelter and medicine for people in crisis.
Items with both civilian and possible military uses.
Penalties, like trade bans, that countries use to pressure another government.
